input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_summary: Describe how JSON-constrained outputs and explicit evidence injection improve auditability and reproducibility; propose extensions (richer graph encodings, multi-stage retrieval, evaluation on larger/other domains) and outline next steps for tooling and evaluation to facilitate community adoption.

Multi-aspect dense retrieval aims to incorporate aspect information (e.g., brand and category) into dual encoders to facilitate relevance matching. As an early and representative multi-aspect dense retriever, MADRAL learns several extra aspect embeddings and fuses the explicit aspects with an implicit aspect "OTHER" for final representation. MADRAL was evaluated on proprietary data and its code was not released, making it challenging to validate its effectiveness on other datasets. We failed to reproduce its effectiveness on the public MA-Amazon data, motivating us to probe the reasons and re-examine its components. We propose several component alternatives for comparisons, including replacing "OTHER" with "CLS" and representing aspects with the first several content tokens. Through extensive experiments, we confirm that learning "OTHER" from scratch in aspect fusion is harmful. In contrast, our proposed variants can greatly enhance the retrieval performance. Our research not only sheds light on the limitations of MADRAL but also provides valuable insights for future studies on more powerful multi-aspect dense retrieval models. Code will be released at: https://github.com/sunxiaojie99/Reproducibility-for-MADRAL.

[RID:web:paper:98d83212b104] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2301.05174v2" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.05174v2" title="Scene-centric vs. Object-centric Image-Text Cross-modal Retrieval: A Reproducibility Study"
Most approaches to cross-modal retrieval (CMR) focus either on object-centric datasets, meaning that each document depicts or describes a single object, or on scene-centric datasets, meaning that each image depicts or describes a complex scene that involves multiple objects and relations between them. We posit that a robust CMR model should generalize well across both dataset types. Despite recent advances in CMR, the reproducibility of the results and their generalizability across different dataset types has not been studied before. We address this gap and focus on the reproducibility of the state-of-the-art CMR results when evaluated on object-centric and scene-centric datasets. We select two state-of-the-art CMR models with different architectures: (i) CLIP; and (ii) X-VLM. Additionally, we select two scene-centric datasets, and three object-centric datasets, and determine the relative performance of the selected models on these datasets. We focus on reproducibility, replicability, and generalizability of the outcomes of previously published CMR experiments. We discover that the experiments are not fully reproducible and replicable. Besides, the relative performance results partially generalize across object-centric and scene-centric datasets. On top of that, the scores obtained on object-centric datasets are much lower than the scores obtained on scene-centric datasets. For reproducibility and transparency we make our source code and the trained models publicly available.
input.section_draft:
[General background knowledge] The workflow described in this paper is intended to increase auditability and reproducibility by producing machine-readable section artifacts (strict JSON objects) and by making source evidence explicit at the time of generation. Because the outputs encode section text, required metadata, and explicit evidence anchors in a constrained schema, they create a verifiable trail that can be inspected, validated, and re-run by downstream tools or by human reviewers.

[General background knowledge] From a provenance perspective, JSON-constrained sections facilitate deterministic post-hoc checks: automated validators can confirm schema conformance, assert the presence of required citation fields, and flag sections lacking evidence anchors. This machine-checkable interface reduces the need for ad hoc manual parsing of natural-language drafts and lowers the barrier for programmatic auditing of claims and citations.

[General background knowledge] Explicit evidence injection at generation time further supports reproducibility by recording which retrieved documents or snippets were presented to the model when composing each claim. When these retrieved artifacts are preserved alongside the JSON outputs, subsequent auditors can re-run retrieval and scoring pipelines, compare retrieved sets, and determine whether changes in downstream outputs stem from retrieval differences, prompt changes, or model nondeterminism.

In light of these design choices, we identify three complementary directions for tooling and evaluation to encourage community adoption and to strengthen reproducibility guarantees.

1) Standardized validators and export utilities.
[General background knowledge] Providing reference implementations of JSON validators, citation-coverage checkers, and LaTeX exporters lowers friction for adopters. Such utilities should (a) verify required evidence fields for each section, (b) produce human-readable diffs between successive JSON versions, and (c) emit a compiled LaTeX manuscript together with a refs.bib that is traceable to the original retrieved artifacts.

2) Richer graph encodings and inter-section contracts.
We advocate extending the section graph to encode not only dependency structure but also explicit inter-section contracts (e.g., variable definitions, shared claims, and allowed citation scopes). By formalizing the expectations between nodes, automated checks can detect inconsistent reuse of terms or ungrounded references that violate declared contracts. These richer encodings would also enable finer-grained scheduling policies and targeted re-generation of affected nodes when upstream content changes.

3) Multi-stage and auditable retrieval pipelines.
Recording and exposing the retrieval pipeline (queries, ranking scores, and selection thresholds) is essential for reproducibility. Future work should integrate multi-stage retrieval logs into the JSON outputs so that auditors can (a) reproduce the retrieval context that led to each evidence anchor and (b) evaluate how retrieval choices impact unsupported assertions. Implementations should support deterministic replay of retrieval steps where feasible.

4) Evaluation at scale and cross-domain replication.
To move from design claims to robust empirical conclusions, broader evaluations on diverse topical domains and larger document sets are needed. Such evaluations should prioritize metrics that directly reflect auditability and reproducibility (for example, repeatability of retrieval results given fixed indices and deterministic seeds, and stability of citation coverage under controlled perturbations). Public benchmarks and shared datasets will be important to enable community comparison and to surface domain-specific failure modes.

5) Human-in-the-loop workflows and policy controls.
Practical adoption will require lightweight human review interfaces that expose the JSON artifacts and retrieved evidence without obscuring context. We recommend integrating annotation layers for human reviewers to mark unsupported claims, attach corrective evidence, and trigger selective re-generation. Additionally, explicit policy controls (e.g., thresholds for allowed paraphrase of cited material) help align automated generation with editorial standards.

Limitations and cautionary notes.
[General background knowledge] The proposed improvements to auditability and reproducibility rely on stable retrieval indices, preserved evidence artifacts, and consistent tooling for validation and export. If any of these components are unavailable or change unpredictably, the practical benefits will be reduced. Thus, promoting reproducible practices requires both methodological design (as described) and infrastructural commitments (versioned indices, preserved artifacts, and open tooling).

Concluding remarks and immediate next steps.
As practical next steps toward community adoption, we propose (a) releasing reference JSON schemas and validator code, (b) publishing a small reproducible example that demonstrates the end-to-end pipeline with retrieval logs and compiled LaTeX, and (c) initiating a shared benchmark for citation-fidelity and reproducibility checks. These deliverables aim to make it straightforward for others to reproduce experiments, audit generated sections, and extend the graph-aware prompting paradigm in new domains.
